prize_parts.citation: For the conception, construction and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments, which made possible the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B020 as my preferred single-part prize. The science has not been questioned by anyone: a particle predicted in 1964 was found in 2012 by two independent detectors, the Standard Model was completed, and a decade of coupling and mass measurements has made the result fully mature. The 2013 prize honoured the theoretical proposal, so the observation itself is unrecognised, and I judge the two achievements distinct. Round 1 showed that the real dispute is attribution, so I now state the rule explicitly. The prize honours the people without whom neither detector would have existed and whose projects made a discovery of this kind possible: the founders and long-term leaders of the two experiments, in the conception and construction phase. By that rule the ATLAS and CMS founding spokespersons, Jenni and Della Negra, are required, and Virdee, who led CMS construction as project leader and whose design choices underlie the discovery channels, is the third name. The citation names both experiments, so the prize is not read as honouring one collaboration. This rule is something that can be written down and applied, which is more than can be said for leadership at the moment of announcement, because that role rotates every two years and honours timing as much as contribution.
statement.case_against: A three-person cut across two collaborations of thousands remains the weakest allocation on the shortlist, and the 2 CMS plus 1 ATLAS split is unbalanced, as Danielsson and Lindroth pointed out. A prize for construction and project leadership can be read as honouring management, not a specific scientific insight, and Mehlig, Olsson and Lindroth hold this view seriously. The risk that the committee sees the Higgs observation as a continuation of the 2013 prize cannot be dismissed. My instrumentalist preference and my doctoral work at an accelerator laboratory make me the member most likely to overrate this entry, so I discount my own ranking. If the committee cannot accept a leadership-based rule, B020 should not be awarded this year and B001 is the better choice.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, arguing that Gianotti's role as ATLAS spokesperson at the time of the announcement is the most visible link to the 2012 result, and asked the Chair to push on the choice of names.
responses.response: I have pushed on it and still prefer Virdee. Spokesperson at the announcement is a two-year elected role, so on that logic the credit goes to whoever held the chair that year, which is a weaker basis than who made the detectors work. Virdee was project leader of CMS through construction, which carries scientific and technical responsibility for the apparatus in a way the announcement role does not. I accept that this leaves ATLAS with only Jenni and I regard the imbalance as the price of any three-name cut. I would not treat the Gianotti substitution as a point of principle, and if the committee prefers the announcement-based rule I would join a configuration of Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni rather than block B020. The question the committee must settle is the rule, not the name.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B020 only if the committee can agree a principled credit rule, and notes that the different name sets in the openings signal that no obvious triple exists.
responses.response: This is the right test and I have tried to meet it. The rule I propose is conception and construction leadership, written into a citation that names both experiments, and it yields Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee without reference to who was visible in 2012. I accept that different members will weigh the rule differently, and that the spread of names in the openings reflects real ambiguity, not obvious error. Where I disagree is that this makes B020 uniquely difficult: B001 requires a cut from five to three with an unresolved theory-versus-experiment split between Zoller and Esslinger, which your own uncertainties list shows is just as contestable. If the committee cannot accept my rule, I would rather say so openly than hide the problem in a looser citation.

responses.point: Lindroth holds that a three-person Higgs prize rewards leadership roles rather than a specific scientific contribution and that B013 has a two-person credit that maps directly onto the idea and its realisation.
responses.response: I agree that B013 has the cleaner attribution on the shortlist, and the idea-to-realisation mapping of Katori and Ye is a real strength. We still differ on what the achievement is. In the Higgs case the discovery depended on instruments that took two decades to design and build, so the leadership of those projects is a scientific contribution, not an administrative one, because the detector performance sets what could be seen. I also keep B013 as my second alternative because I share your view that the control of systematics is the substance, but I weigh a decade of confirmed Higgs measurements above the pending redefinition of the second. Clean credit should count for much, but I do not think it should override a difference in scientific consequence.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B020 sixth because a three-person cut across two collaborations of thousands is the weakest allocation of any shortlisted candidate, while regarding B041 as defensible if the citation is built around the discovery.
responses.response: I accept the comparison on allocation, and I do not dispute that B041 has the more natural theory-plus-experiment structure, with Bistritzer and MacDonald for the prediction and Jarillo-Herrero for the observation. However, you and Eriksson both list the omission of Cao and Dean and the unsettled pairing mechanism as real reservations, and you are willing to see B001 chosen if the committee finds B041 early. Eight years is short next to the Higgs and cold-atom results, and waiting costs little. A weak allocation in a mature field seems to me a better problem than a clean allocation in a field still in motion, though I accept that this is a judgement and not a measurement.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B011 to B001 and proposes Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, with a mixed theory-plus-experiment citation, and says quantum advantage has not yet been shown.
responses.response: Your move helps answer the chair question about not rewarding Cirac and Zoller twice, because crediting Zoller inside B001 absorbs the B011 argument and removes the need for a two-part prize. I find that coherent. My concern is that the mixed prize rests on priority between Zoller and Jaksch for the lattice proposal, which you say you have not verified, and that Esslinger is then excluded despite the fermionic Hubbard realisation. I therefore keep B001 as my first alternative and will support it if B020 fails, but I would want the committee to settle the Zoller-versus-Esslinger choice explicitly before the vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts conception and construction leadership as a ground for a prize, or insists on an announcement-based or contribution-based rule, which would change the third name from Virdee to Gianotti or remove B020 from contention.
Whether the 2 CMS plus 1 ATLAS split is acceptable or whether balance across the two experiments should outweigh my construction-based rule.
Whether the committee judges the Higgs observation sufficiently distinct from the 2013 prize.
Whether the unresolved Zoller-versus-Esslinger choice in B001 can be settled by the committee, since that determines my fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented collaboration with any credited person on any shortlisted entry: my collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur. My doctoral work at Birmingham and CERN was in experimental particle physics, but my profile does not identify the experiment, so I cannot say whether it involved any credited person, and I disclose that. I disclose again my instrumentalist preference for detector-driven discovery, which most affects B020 and for which colleagues should discount my ranking. As Chair I claim no special knowledge of ATLAS or CMS internal roles.
